name: Odin at Mimir's well: trading an eye for a drink
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The most famous trade in Norse myth. T1: ODIN is the ALL-FATHER, chief of the AESIR gods, lord of Asgard, god of wisdom, poetry, war, and death. He is called ONE-EYE and GRIMNIR ('the Masked One') among many names; his hall is VALHALLA, where his chosen slain feast until Ragnarok. T2: beneath one of the three roots of the world tree YGGDRASIL lies a well guarded by the wise old giant MIMIR, whose water grants WISDOM to whoever drinks it (Snorri, Gylfaginning 15). No one may drink from it without paying Mimir's price. T3: Odin comes to the well and asks for a drink. Mimir names his price: ONE OF ODIN'S EYES, dropped into the well as a pledge. Odin plucks out his own eye, casts it into the water, and drinks (Voluspa 28-29; Gylfaginning 15). From that day he is called the ONE-EYED god, and his lost eye rests forever at the bottom of Mimir's well. T4: after the war between the Aesir and the Vanir, Mimir is beheaded and Odin embalms the SEVERED HEAD with herbs and sings spells over it; the head speaks to him thereafter and gives him counsel from the well (Snorri, Ynglinga Saga 4, 7). T5: the story is the working image of Norse WISDOM AS COST -- Odin does not receive knowledge as a gift; he PAYS for it in his own body, and he keeps paying (see the runes ladder). The Voluspa's seeress opens her prophecy with the line that she knows where Odin's eye is hidden -- 'in Mimir's famous well' (Voluspa 28) -- because the eye is still there, still pledged. Further rungs: Odin's OTHER names run to more than 170 (Grimnismal is a catalogue of them -- Har the High, Jafnhar the Just-as-High, Third, Hangatyr the Hanged-One's-God, Bolverk the Ill-Worker); Mimir's severed head is one of the Aesir's most treasured possessions in the sagas; Odin's wife is FRIGG, who alone shares his high seat HLIDSKJALF from which all worlds can be seen.

Dinner-test payoff: T3 (he plucked out his OWN EYE and dropped it in a well to buy a drink) and T4 (later he embalmed the well-guardian's SEVERED HEAD and it talked back to him). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Christ paying with his body or of Prometheus paying with his liver -- wisdom-at-a-price is the Norse pattern. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Odin sacrifices (his hanging on Yggdrasil for the runes -- ADJACENT-real, own ladder; the Mead of Poetry -- own ladder), other one-eyed figures (Polyphemus the Cyclops -- Greek pillar), other wisdom-well figures (Urd's well beneath a different root -- own ladder). Wrong body-parts: not a hand (that is Tyr), not a finger (that is Fionn -- Celtic).

name: Odin on Yggdrasil: nine nights for the runes
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The self-hanging of the All-Father, given verbatim in the Havamal. T1: Odin, who had already given an eye for wisdom, seeks a deeper knowledge yet -- the RUNES, the magical letter-signs that shape fate. To win them he must undergo a self-sacrifice unlike any the gods have known. T2: he goes to the world tree YGGDRASIL (the very name means 'Ygg's horse' -- Ygg 'the Terrible' is one of Odin's names, and the tree becomes his gallows). He STRINGS HIMSELF UP by the neck from a branch, pierced through the side by HIS OWN SPEAR GUNGNIR, and hangs there for NINE NIGHTS (Havamal 138). T3: no one takes him down, no one gives him food, no one gives him a drink from a horn. He hangs in the wind, wounded and thirsty, without offering to any god -- 'given to Odin, myself given to myself' (Havamal 138: 'gefinn Odni, sjalfr sjalfum mer'). T4: on the ninth night he SCREAMS out and takes up the runes and falls back down from the tree with them. He has learned the runes and 'nine mighty songs' (Havamal 139-141), and the runes will belong to gods, elves, dwarves, and men forever after through him. T5: the whole sequence is quoted verbatim in the RUNATAL section of the Havamal ('Sayings of the High One'), stanzas 138-145 -- Odin himself is the speaker: 'I know that I hung on a windy tree / nine long nights / wounded with a spear, dedicated to Odin / myself to myself / on that tree of which no man knows / from where its roots run.' It is the plainest single statement of pay-with-your-body wisdom in the Norse corpus. Further rungs: the Havamal is preserved in the CODEX REGIUS manuscript (c. 1270); the parallel to a hanged-god-on-a-tree with a spear wound has drawn every kind of Christian-comparative reading -- honest scholars treat it as a Norse motif documented in its own right; Gungnir the spear was made by the sons of Ivaldi, the same dwarves who made Sif's golden hair.
source: PRIMARY: Poetic Edda, Havamal 138-145 (the Runatal section -- the whole self-hanging + rune-taking, esp. stanza 138 verbatim 'I know that I hung on a windy tree nine long nights wounded with a spear, given to Odin, myself given to myself'). Also Havamal 146-163 (Odin's list of the eighteen charms he learned). Snorri does not retell this scene directly. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Havamal' and 'Runatal' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Havamal', 'Yggdrasil', 'Runes' -- Odin hanging himself nine nights on Yggdrasil pierced by his own spear, given to himself, learning the runes, Runatal section, Codex Regius manuscript. framing_note: The most quoted single passage in Norse poetry -- MUST use the Havamal 138 verbatim quote in the T5 ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (he hanged HIMSELF, pierced by his OWN spear, for NINE NIGHTS) and T3 ('given to Odin, myself given to myself'). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem quote the 'myself to myself' line AND ask who is speaking; describe the SCENE (a god on a tree in the wind, a spear-wound in his side, nine nights without water) and let the recall be the god, the tree's name, or the number of nights. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: this is the passage that most invites Christ-comparisons -- resist. Tell it as Norse. The Norse pattern is 'a god pays HIS OWN BODY for HIS OWN wisdom, and the tree is the world-tree' -- do not gloss it as prefiguring anything. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Odin sacrifices (the eye at Mimir's -- ADJACENT-real, own ladder; the Mead of Poetry), other tree-hangings (Absalom in his hair from an oak -- OT), other numbers of nights (three like Jonah, forty like Christ in the wilderness -- adjacent-real from the OTHER pillar). Wrong spear-names: not Draupnir (that is the ring), not Gram (Sigurd's sword), not Mistilteinn (mistletoe / Balder).

name: Huginn and Muninn: thought and memory
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The two ravens that fly the world for Odin. T1: Odin sits on his high seat in Asgard and cannot see everywhere at once. To fix this he keeps TWO RAVENS, who fly out over Midgard every dawn and return at breakfast to whisper what they have seen into his ears. T2: their names are HUGINN and MUNINN -- HUGINN means 'THOUGHT' and MUNINN means 'MEMORY' (Snorri, Gylfaginning 38). It is because of these ravens that Odin is called RAFNAGUD, 'Raven-God'. T3: they fly out over the whole world (Old Norse 'jormungrund', 'great earth') at day's first light and are back at dagmal, the morning meal (Grimnismal 20). Every day, all worlds; every evening, the debrief. T4: Odin quietly worries about them. Grimnismal 20 has him saying: 'For Huginn I fear lest he come not home, but I fear yet more for Muninn.' Even the All-Father is more afraid of losing MEMORY than of losing THOUGHT. T5: the two ravens are one of the OLDEST and most-attested Odin markers -- carved on 6th-8th c. helmet plates from Vendel and Torslunda in Sweden, and painted onto the Oseberg tapestry beside a spear-carrying figure. Whenever a Norse warrior sees a raven-cloud following an army he knows Odin is nearby. Further rungs: Odin also keeps TWO WOLVES at his feet in Valhalla, GERI ('Greedy') and FREKI ('Ravenous'), who eat all the food set before him while he himself lives on wine alone (Grimnismal 19 -- see the wolves ladder); the two ravens and two wolves are always paired in Norse iconography; Odin's throne HLIDSKJALF sees everything, but the ravens hear things Hlidskjalf cannot.

Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the two ravens are named THOUGHT and MEMORY) and T4 (the All-Father is more scared of losing memory than of losing thought). name: Sleipnir: the eight-legged horse
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The strangest steed in the Nine Worlds and how it was born. T1: Odin rides a horse called SLEIPNIR, and Sleipnir has EIGHT LEGS. He is the fastest horse in all the worlds and can gallop on land, on sea, and through the air (Snorri, Gylfaginning 15, 42). T2: Sleipnir's mother is LOKI. This is the story: a stranger comes to Asgard offering to build the gods a wall around their city in a single winter, asking as payment the sun, the moon, and the goddess FREYJA. The gods agree only on the impossible condition that the WALL-BUILDER work alone with no help but his STALLION SVADILFARI (Gylfaginning 42). T3: the stallion turns out to be almost as good as a workman on his own, and the wall goes up so fast the gods realise they are going to lose Freyja, the sun, and the moon. They corner LOKI (whose idea the deal had been) and tell him to fix it or die. T4: Loki turns himself into a MARE and comes trotting out of the woods; Svadilfari the stallion breaks his harness and gallops after her, and the two of them run off into the forest for a long night. The wall is not finished in time; the builder (revealed as a giant) is killed by Thor with the hammer. Some months later Loki returns to Asgard leading a foal -- an EIGHT-LEGGED grey COLT called SLEIPNIR, and hands him to Odin as a gift (Gylfaginning 42). T5: Sleipnir is the only horse that can go the road to HEL and come back. When Baldr dies (see that ladder), it is Odin's son HERMODR who borrows Sleipnir and rides him for NINE NIGHTS down the road to Hel through 'valleys deep and dark' and leaps the fence of Helheim to bargain for Baldr -- and it is Sleipnir's eight-hooved leap that clears the gate. Further rungs: Sleipnir is depicted on the 8th-c. TJANGVIDE picture-stone from Gotland, carrying a rider into a hall where a woman with a horn waits -- almost certainly Odin arriving at Valhalla; the name Sleipnir means SLIPPY or SLIDER; the eight legs are still an unsolved puzzle for scholars (a bier carried by four pallbearers = eight legs? a shamanic-trance image?).
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 15 (Sleipnir the best of horses), Gylfaginning 42 (the wall-builder story, Loki as mare, birth of Sleipnir), Gylfaginning 49 (Hermodr rides Sleipnir to Hel over nine nights). Also Voluspa Hin Skamma. name: The Mead of Poetry: Odin as an eagle
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The theft that gave the Norse world its poetry, told in Snorri's Skaldskaparmal. T1: after the Aesir-Vanir war, both sides spat into a jar to seal the peace, and out of the spittle they made a wise being named KVASIR. Kvasir walked the earth answering questions until two dwarves, FJALAR and GALAR, murdered him and drained his blood into three vessels -- a cauldron called ODRERIR and two jars, SON and BODN. Mixed with honey the blood became the MEAD OF POETRY, and anyone who drank it became a poet or a wise man (Skaldskaparmal 5-6). T2: the mead ended up with a giant called SUTTUNG, who hid it inside the mountain HNITBJORG with his daughter GUNNLOD set to guard it. Odin decided to get it. He came to the mountain in disguise, bored a hole through the rock with an AUGER called RATI, turned himself into a SNAKE and slid inside (Skaldskaparmal 6; Havamal 104-110). T3: inside, Odin found Gunnlod, spent THREE NIGHTS with her, and in return she let him take THREE DRINKS of the mead -- one drink from each vessel. In three long swallows he drank ALL THREE dry (Skaldskaparmal 6; Havamal 105). T4: with the mead in his throat, Odin turned into an EAGLE and flew back to Asgard as fast as his wings could carry him. Suttung saw him, turned into an eagle himself, and gave chase. Odin barely made it over the walls of Asgard; the Aesir set out jars to catch what he spat up. T5: Odin spat the mead into the jars for the gods to keep -- but in his panic-flight he also let a few DROPS FLY OUT BEHIND him. Those drops are known as the SKALDFIFLA HLUT, 'the poetaster's share' -- the mead of BAD poets, dropped from Odin's fear-loosened tail; anyone who ever wrote bad verse got their gift from those back-drops (Skaldskaparmal 6). Ever since, GOOD poetry is called 'Odin's mead', 'Kvasir's blood', 'the drink of the dwarves'; that back-story is the whole vocabulary of skaldic poetry. Further rungs: the auger is named RATI ('gnawer'); the two jars are BODN and SON, the cauldron is ODRERIR; Havamal 13-14 is Odin remembering he got drunk at Fjalar's hall, and Havamal 104-110 remembers his three nights with Gunnlod; Norse kennings for poetry -- 'Kvasir's blood', 'Odin's booty', 'the dwarves' drink', 'the mead of Hnitbjorg' -- all point back to this one story.

Dinner-test payoff: T5 (bad poetry is called 'the poetaster's share' because it comes from what Odin dropped BEHIND HIM while fleeing as an eagle) and T3 (he drank THREE VESSELS DRY IN THREE SWALLOWS). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Odin as an eagle stealing the mead' AND ask what he turned into; describe the SCENE (a mountain, a giant's daughter, three vessels, an eagle chase, jars set out to catch spit) and let the recall be the BIRD, the girl's name, the vessel-names, or WHERE bad-poet-mead comes from. name: Odin the wanderer: the Wild Hunt
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The god who walks the world in a broad hat and leads a ghost-army through the sky. T1: Odin is the WANDERING god. He puts on a broad-brimmed HAT pulled low over his eye, wraps himself in a dark BLUE CLOAK, leans on a walking-staff, and travels the roads of Midgard in disguise (he calls himself GRIMNIR, 'the Masked One', in the Grimnismal, and GANGLERI, 'the Wanderer', in Snorri's frame-story for Gylfaginning). T2: on stormy winter nights, especially between YULE (mid-December) and Twelfth Night, farmers across the Germanic world once said they could hear a ghostly HUNT thundering through the sky overhead -- hounds baying, hoofbeats, a wild rider with a spear, a horde of the dead riding with him. This is the OSKORREI or WILD HUNT, and the leader is Odin. T3: to see the Wild Hunt was an omen -- of war, of plague, or of a good harvest to come, depending on the region; to be caught in its path was to be swept along and never come home. In Germany the leader was sometimes called the 'wild army' (das wutende Heer, from Odin's German name Wodan), in Scandinavia it was Odin riding Sleipnir with his ravens overhead. T4: Odin's wanderer-disguise is the reason he needs so many NAMES -- Grimnismal (the 'Sayings of the Masked One') is a whole poem in which King Geirroth's captive prisoner refuses to give his name and instead recites forty-plus names of Odin ('Har the High, Jafnhar Just-as-High, Third, Bolverk Ill-Worker, Hangatyr God-of-the-Hanged, Grimnir the Masked, Ganglari the Wanderer ...') until the king realises with horror that he has just been TORTURING the All-Father, staggers backward onto his own drawn sword, and dies. T5: the Wild Hunt lasted in FOLK memory for a thousand years after the conversion, still ridden in Scandinavian and German villages under names like OSKOREIA and DE WILDE JAGD. In some later Christian versions the huntsman is King Herla, King Arthur, or Herne with antlers -- but in the earliest Germanic form it is Odin on Sleipnir with the dead. Further rungs: the very common Odin-image -- old man, one eye, broad hat, cloak, staff -- is the source of both Tolkien's Gandalf and countless later grey-wanderer wizards; the Norse verb 'ganga' means 'to wander' -- from Ganglari; the raven-and-wolves ride with him on the hunt.
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning frame (Odin as three thrones -- Har, Jafnhar, Third -- receiving the wanderer Gangleri); Poetic Edda, Grimnismal (whole poem -- Odin bound between two fires in Geirroth's hall recites his own names until Geirroth falls on his sword). Secondary Norse and German folk-tradition: Jakob Grimm, Deutsche Mythologie ch. 31 (the Wild Hunt survivals across Germany). name: Mjolnir: the hammer of Thor
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The most famous weapon in Norse myth and how it was made. T1: THOR is the son of Odin and JORD (Earth), god of THUNDER and defender of Asgard and Midgard against the giants. His weapon is a HAMMER called MJOLNIR ('crusher'), which returns to his hand whenever he throws it and can be shrunk small enough to hide in his shirt (Snorri, Gylfaginning 21). Its stroke makes the lightning; his goats pulling his chariot make the thunder. T2: Mjolnir was forged by the dwarf brothers SINDRI and BROKKR in a wager against Loki. Loki had bet his own head that the sons of Ivaldi (another dwarf-team) could make finer treasures than Sindri and Brokkr could. Sindri put a pig-skin in the forge and told Brokkr to work the bellows without stopping (Skaldskaparmal 43). T3: Loki, panicking, turned himself into a horsefly and BIT BROKKR three times -- on the hand, on the neck, and finally between the eyes so blood ran down and Brokkr let go of the bellows just for a heartbeat. That heartbeat is why Mjolnir came out of the forge with a SHORT HANDLE -- perfectly balanced, but too short to swing two-handed (Skaldskaparmal 43). T4: even so the hammer was so obviously the best of the six treasures made that day (with GULLINBURSTI the golden boar for Freyr and DRAUPNIR the ring for Odin also from Sindri and Brokkr) that the gods judged Loki had lost the bet. Loki wriggled out with a lawyer's trick -- the dwarves could take his head but could not touch his neck (not part of the wager), so instead they sewed his LIPS SHUT with a leather thong called VARTARI. T5: Mjolnir is Asgard's ONLY guarantee against the giants: without it Thor is not Thor. It is also SACRED -- it consecrates births, marriages, and funerals (in Snorri, Thor raises Mjolnir over Baldr's funeral pyre to hallow it, Gylfaginning 49). Grave-goods across Viking-age Scandinavia are hung with small silver hammer-pendants (Mjolnir amulets) worn as protection -- so many of them survive that they are the most-collected single Viking artifact type. Further rungs: Thor needs two other pieces of gear to swing Mjolnir -- an iron gauntlet called JARNGREIPR and a belt called MEGINGJORD that doubles his strength (own further rung); the hammer is small enough to hide under Thor's tunic (which becomes important in the Thrymskvida ladder); Mjolnir is one of THREE named artifacts Sindri and Brokkr make in the same forging session.

name: Thor's goats: eaten at supper, alive at dawn

T2: the goats have an astonishing property: Thor can SLAUGHTER THEM, ROAST THEM, EAT THEM at dinner, and as long as the bones are all carefully laid out on the hide, he can wave his HAMMER over them the next morning and they come BACK TO LIFE ready to be harnessed again (Gylfaginning 44). T4: the farmer's son, a boy called THIALFI, is hungry for the marrow and CANNOT RESIST -- he splits a THIGH BONE with his knife to suck out the marrow, and lays the split bone back on the hide with the others (Gylfaginning 44). T5: the next morning Thor waves Mjolnir over the goat-hides, and the goats stand up alive -- but one of them is LAME in a hind leg. Thor sees what has happened, and his brows come down so low his hair covers his eyes; his knuckles turn white on Mjolnir. The peasant family drop to their knees begging for mercy, and to pay the debt they give Thor their TWO CHILDREN, Thialfi and his sister ROSKVA, who become Thor's servants forever after (Gylfaginning 44). name: Thor and Jormungandr: fishing with Hymir
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The day Thor hooked the Midgard Serpent, told in Hymiskvida and Snorri. T1: JORMUNGANDR is the MIDGARD SERPENT, one of the three monstrous children of Loki (with Fenrir the wolf and Hel the death-goddess). Odin threw him into the sea around Midgard when he was small, and he grew so long he now WRAPS THE WORLD and holds his own tail in his teeth (Snorri, Gylfaginning 34, 47). He is the eternal enemy of Thor. T2: one morning Thor goes to visit the giant HYMIR to borrow the huge CAULDRON Aegir the sea-god needs to brew ale for the whole Aesir (Hymiskvida; parallel in Gylfaginning 48). Hymir agrees only if Thor helps him row out and catch enough fish for supper. Thor asks Hymir for bait; Hymir tells him to get his own. Thor walks into Hymir's cattle-pasture and RIPS THE HEAD OFF Hymir's biggest ox, a black bull called HIMINHRJOTR ('Heaven-Bellower'). T3: Thor takes the ox-head down to the boat and rows out with Hymir. Thor rows so hard and so far past Hymir's usual fishing-ground that Hymir goes pale -- they are now over the abyss where the serpent lives (Gylfaginning 48). Thor baits an iron hook with the ox-head and drops it. T4: Jormungandr takes the bait. Thor braces his feet against the hull of the boat, and his heels PUNCH STRAIGHT THROUGH the planks so that he is standing on the sea floor as he heaves. He heaves the head of Jormungandr right up out of the water -- the serpent glares at him with poison dripping from its jaws (Gylfaginning 48). Thor reaches for Mjolnir. T5: Hymir, TERRIFIED, cuts the line with his knife -- and the serpent sinks back into the sea. Thor turns and knocks Hymir overboard with his fist. In Snorri's version the giant survives; in the Hymiskvida the ending is left open. The whole scene is CARVED IN STONE on the 8th-c. Further rungs: Jormungandr will meet Thor a SECOND time at Ragnarok, and there Thor will kill him and stagger nine paces before dying of his poison (Voluspa 55-56); Hymir's cauldron is a mile deep; Thor's smashed-through boat-hull is a common motif in the picture-stones.

name: Thrymskvida: Thor in a wedding-veil
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The comic epic of Thor recovering his stolen hammer, told in the Poetic Edda's Thrymskvida. T1: Thor wakes one morning to find MJOLNIR is GONE. He shakes his beard, his hair, his temper is coming up; he sends Loki out to find it (Thrymskvida 1-2). T2: Loki borrows Freyja's FALCON-CLOAK and flies out over the worlds. He finds the hammer in the hands of the giant-king THRYM ('Din'), who admits he has hidden Mjolnir 'eight leagues under the earth' and will return it only on ONE CONDITION: he wants to marry FREYJA and have her brought to Jotunheim as his bride (Thrymskvida 6-8). T3: Freyja hears the demand and snorts so hard her BRISINGAMEN, the famous necklace, snaps off her neck (Thrymskvida 13). She refuses absolutely. The gods hold council. HEIMDALLR (in some manuscripts LOKI) proposes the only plan that will work: THOR MUST GO in a bride's gown and veil and pretend to be Freyja himself. Thor bellows in protest -- the Aesir will call him womanish forever after (Thrymskvida 17). Loki tells him if he doesn't, Thrym will move in. T4: Thor dresses. Bridal linen, keys at the belt, JEWELS on his broad chest, the BRISINGAMEN around his neck, a wedding VEIL over his beard. Loki puts on a maid's dress and goes with him as the bride's handmaiden. They ride to Jotunheim in Thor's goat-chariot (Thrymskvida 19-21). At the wedding feast Thor eats an OX, EIGHT SALMON, all the DAINTIES set aside for the women, and drinks THREE HORNS of mead. Thrym is amazed and Loki (as the maid) explains sweetly that the bride had 'not eaten for eight nights, so keen was she to come to Jotunheim' (Thrymskvida 26). Thrym leans over to kiss his bride and jerks back at her BURNING EYES; Loki explains she has 'not slept for eight nights, so keen was she' (Thrymskvida 28). T5: at last Thrym, delighted, calls for MJOLNIR TO BE LAID IN HIS BRIDE'S LAP to hallow the wedding (Thrymskvida 30). The hammer is brought. Thor's hand closes on it. He rises up under the veil, and the wedding-hall becomes a slaughterhouse -- Thor kills Thrym FIRST, then his sister who was asking for a bride-gift, then every giant in the hall (Thrymskvida 31-32). The poem ends: 'thus Odin's son got his hammer back' (Thrymskvida 32). Further rungs: Thrymskvida is preserved ONLY in the Codex Regius and is one of the most complete comic set-pieces in the Poetic Edda; the poem is a favourite for schoolchildren in Iceland to this day; the trick has echoes in the later Grettis saga.

name: Thor at Utgardaloki: the horn, the cat, and the old woman
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The trick-castle where Thor fought and lost three impossible contests, told in Gylfaginning. T1: Thor and Loki, with the boy THIALFI, set out east into Jotunheim. On the road they sleep one night in what turns out to be the empty THUMB OF A GIANT'S GLOVE (the giant SKRYMIR, whose real size Thor cannot fathom, was napping beside them). They reach a colossal castle called UTGARD, whose gate is so high they slip in between the bars, and are received by its king, UTGARDALOKI (Gylfaginning 45-47). T2: Utgardaloki mocks them: none of them looks like much. To be worthy of a place at his table each must do some feat. LOKI is challenged to EAT faster than a man called LOGI; they set two troughs of meat between them, and Logi finishes first because he has eaten the meat, the bones, AND the trough. THIALFI is set to RUN a footrace against a boy called HUGI on the courtyard track; Hugi outstrips him by such a distance that when Thialfi arrives at the finish Hugi is already coming back to meet him. T3: THOR is offered three tests. First, he must DRAIN a DRINKING HORN in one, two, or (at worst) three swallows. Thor pulls at it and pulls and the drink barely goes down at all. He tries three long-pull swallows and the horn is still nearly full (Gylfaginning 46). T4: second, he must LIFT the king's CAT off the floor. It is a large grey cat curled on the flagstones. Thor gets his arm under it and heaves; the cat merely arches its back until one PAW comes off the ground, and Thor has to admit defeat (Gylfaginning 46). Third, Thor is offered to WRESTLE the king's old nurse, a hag called ELLI. Thor closes with her and she plants her feet; the harder he pulls, the firmer she stands, until she brings him DOWN ON ONE KNEE, and Utgardaloki calls the match (Gylfaginning 46). T5: the next morning Utgardaloki walks the guests out of Utgard and tells them the truth. Loki's opponent LOGI was WILDFIRE -- fire eats trough and all. Thialfi's opponent HUGI was THOUGHT -- and nothing can outrun thought. The horn Thor could not drain had its lower end IN THE SEA, and Thor's three swallows had drawn the ocean down so far it created the TIDES. The cat Thor almost lifted was JORMUNGANDR THE MIDGARD SERPENT, and by making one paw come up Thor had nearly heaved the world-serpent off the earth. And ELLI, whom Thor could not throw, was OLD AGE, whom no one has ever wrestled to a fall; that Thor came down only on one knee is astonishing (Gylfaginning 47). And with that Utgardaloki DISAPPEARS -- when Thor turns to swing Mjolnir at him, castle and king and all are gone; there is only the plain (Gylfaginning 47). Further rungs: Skrymir on the road turns out to be Utgardaloki himself in disguise, and the mountain Thor had spent the night hammering with Mjolnir turns out to be a mountain Utgardaloki had put between himself and Thor's strokes -- the three great valleys Thor left in it are still there.

name: Hrungnir: the whetstone in Thor's forehead
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The duel that gave Thor a permanent souvenir, told in Skaldskaparmal. T1: HRUNGNIR is the strongest of the giants, a stone-giant with a stone HEART, a stone HEAD, and a stone SHIELD; his weapon is a great WHETSTONE (a stone rod used for sharpening blades). He is proud of his horse GULLFAXI ('Golden-Mane'), which he claims outruns even Sleipnir (Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 17). T2: after boasting in Asgard that he will kill all the gods, drown Freyja and Sif in his drinking, and take Valhalla back to Jotunheim, Hrungnir is challenged by Thor to a formal DUEL on the field of Griotunagardar. The giants build him a HELPER -- a giant clay man nine leagues tall and three leagues wide called MOKKURKALFI ('mist-calf') with the heart of a mare stuffed into him; the mare-heart is why the clay-giant TREMBLES when he sees Thor coming (Skaldskaparmal 17). T3: Thor comes at Hrungnir in a thunder-run, with Thialfi ahead of him. Thialfi shouts across to Hrungnir that Thor is coming UP FROM UNDER THE GROUND -- and Hrungnir, panicked, puts his stone shield UNDER HIS FEET to stand on. That is a mistake. Thor comes over the horizon overhead, sees Hrungnir standing on his own shield, and throws MJOLNIR. Hrungnir throws his WHETSTONE at Thor at the same instant. T4: the two thrown weapons COLLIDE in the air. Mjolnir SHATTERS the whetstone -- and shards of it fly in all directions. One large SHARD sinks straight into THOR'S FOREHEAD and lodges there. The rest of the whetstone drops in fragments across the earth -- and every WHETSTONE in the world afterwards is a piece of Hrungnir's stone (Skaldskaparmal 17). Mjolnir flies on and shatters Hrungnir's stone head; Hrungnir falls, and his leg lands ACROSS Thor's neck, pinning him. Only Thor's three-year-old son MAGNI ('Mighty') can lift the leg off. T5: Thor gets home with the WHETSTONE-SHARD STILL IN HIS HEAD. A wise-woman called GROA (mother of the hero Aurvandil) is called in to sing charms over it, and the shard begins to loosen. But partway through the healing, Thor -- meaning to please her -- announces that he has met her husband Aurvandil, carried him across the icy river Elivagar in a basket, and thrown Aurvandil's frozen TOE up into the sky where it now shines as the star called AURVANDIL'S TOE. Groa is so overcome with joy at the news of her husband that she FORGETS THE CHARM -- and the shard STAYS in Thor's head forever after (Skaldskaparmal 17). Further rungs: the story is the etymology-origin of every whetstone; Norse skalds are supposed to never throw a whetstone across the fire because it disturbs the shard in Thor's head; Aurvandil's Toe is often identified with the star Rigel or with Corona Borealis by modern commentators (Snorri does not fix it).

scope: The Vanir god of harvest and sunshine and the choice that will cost him his life at Ragnarok, told in the Skirnismal. T1: FREYR is a VANIR god (not Aesir by birth -- given to the Aesir as a hostage after the Vanir war, along with his father NJORD and his sister FREYJA). He is god of SUNSHINE, GOOD WEATHER, HARVEST, PEACE, and FERTILITY; his home is ALFHEIM ('Elf-Home'), given to him at his teething-tooth feast. His two great gifts from the dwarves are the SHIP SKIDBLADNIR (own further rung) and the golden BOAR GULLINBURSTI (own further rung); his weapon is a magical SWORD that swings itself against giants (Snorri, Gylfaginning 24). T2: one day Freyr sneaks onto Odin's high seat HLIDSKJALF (which no one but Odin and Frigg is supposed to sit on) and looks out. He sees, far away in the north in JOTUNHEIM, a giantess named GERDR walking out of her father's hall -- and when she raises her arm to open a door, the LIGHT REFLECTED FROM HER BARE ARM makes the sea and the sky shine. Freyr comes home from Hlidskjalf and is silent, unable to eat, unable to sleep, unable to speak (Skirnismal 4-7; Gylfaginning 37). T3: his servant SKIRNIR ('the Shining One') asks what is wrong and Freyr confesses. Skirnir agrees to ride to Jotunheim as go-between and win Gerdr for him -- but he needs Freyr's SWIFT HORSE that can carry him through the wall of flame around Gerdr's hall, and he needs Freyr's SELF-SWINGING SWORD to protect him on the road. Freyr HANDS OVER BOTH (Skirnismal 8-10). T4: Skirnir reaches Gerdr and offers her ELEVEN GOLDEN APPLES, then the RING DRAUPNIR itself, in exchange for her hand. She refuses both -- the Vanir have gold enough already. Skirnir then draws Freyr's SWORD and threatens to cut off her head; when that doesn't work he pronounces a horrifying CURSE (Skirnismal 27-36) -- Gerdr will be married to a three-headed frost-giant, will pine forever, will be scorned by gods and men, will sit weeping under the giants' gate. Gerdr, terrified, agrees to meet Freyr in NINE NIGHTS in the grove BARRI. Freyr replies -- 'long is one night, longer are two; how can I endure THREE?' (Skirnismal 42), the most famous love-lament in Norse verse. T5: Freyr got Gerdr. But he had GIVEN HIS SWORD AWAY. And at RAGNAROK, when the fire-giant SURT comes riding out of MUSPELHEIM to burn the world with a sword bright as the sun, Freyr will meet him -- SWORDLESS. Freyr is the FIRST of the gods to fall at Ragnarok, killed by Surt because he traded his sword for a bride. It is the most famous 'the cost of your happiness will kill you' story in the Norse corpus (Voluspa 53; Gylfaginning 51). Further rungs: Freyr's teething-gift of Alfheim (Grimnismal 5); the actual name of his servant (Skirnir) shares a root with 'shining'; Freyr's cult was strong in Sweden, especially at Uppsala where the temple statue in Adam of Bremen's 11th c. account showed him with a huge phallus.

name: Skidbladnir and Gullinbursti: the ship in the pocket and the golden boar
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The two greatest gifts the dwarves ever made for Freyr, told in Skaldskaparmal. T1: FREYR, the Vanir god of harvest and sunshine, was given two extraordinary treasures by the DWARVES -- a ship called SKIDBLADNIR and a boar called GULLINBURSTI ('Golden-Bristled'). Both were made in the same forging-wager between two dwarf-teams that produced Thor's Mjolnir (see the Mjolnir ladder): Freyr's ship and boar came from SINDRI and BROKKR (Skaldskaparmal 43). T2: SKIDBLADNIR is the ship that always has a FAIR WIND in her sails as soon as she is launched, and she is BIG ENOUGH to hold all the Aesir together with their weapons and gear (Gylfaginning 43; Skaldskaparmal 43). T3: but her true wonder is that when Freyr is done sailing her, he can FOLD HER UP LIKE A NAPKIN and put her in his pocket (Gylfaginning 43). She is the largest ship in the world and it fits in a fold of cloth. Snorri calls her plainly 'the best of ships' (Gylfaginning 43). T4: GULLINBURSTI is a BOAR made of GOLD (in some versions bristled with actual golden hair), forged (like Mjolnir) in Sindri and Brokkr's forge. Sindri put a PIG-SKIN in the forge, told Brokkr to work the bellows without stopping, and out came Gullinbursti -- a boar who can RUN FASTER through the sky and over the sea than any horse, whose golden bristles LIGHT UP THE NIGHT so that Freyr can ride him through the dark, and who pulls Freyr's CHARIOT (Skaldskaparmal 43). T5: Gullinbursti carries Freyr to BALDR'S FUNERAL when the Aesir gather to burn Baldr's body on the great ship Ringhorni (Gylfaginning 49); the boar was already the sacred animal of the Vanir before this, and boars sacrificed at Yule are FREYR-offerings (the 'sonargoltr', the SACRIFICIAL BOAR at midwinter, with oaths sworn on its bristles). Freyr's second name is YNGVI, ancestor of the Yngling royal line of Sweden, whose kings kept the boar as a royal emblem for centuries. Further rungs: the other name for Gullinbursti is SLIDRUGTANNI ('slashing-tusk'); Draupnir the arm-ring (see own ladder) is made in the same session as Skidbladnir; the folding-ship idea reappears in Celtic legend as Manannan mac Lir's ship Wave-Sweeper -- convergent myth, not borrowed.
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Skaldskaparmal 43 (both treasures forged by Sindri and Brokkr in the wager); Gylfaginning 43 (Skidbladnir big enough for all Aesir, folds like cloth); Gylfaginning 49 (Gullinbursti at Baldr's funeral). Also Grimnismal 43-44 (list of the treasures). Dinner-test payoff: T3 (a ship BIG ENOUGH FOR EVERY GOD folds up small enough to fit in a pocket) and T4 (a boar made of GOLD that runs through the sky and lights up the night with its BRISTLES). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'a ship that folds like cloth' AND ask the ship's name; describe the SCENE (a Vanir god sailing home with a fair wind, or riding a shining creature through midnight sky) and let the recall be the SHIP, the BOAR, or the OWNER. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of the flying carpet in the Arabian Nights or of the Ark of the Covenant portable in the wilderness -- 'wondrous portable' is a universal myth pattern. DISTRACTOR MINE: other named Norse ships (Naglfar the ship of fingernails carrying the dead at Ragnarok -- ADJACENT-real, must not confuse), other named boars (the boar of Ben Bulben in Celtic myth -- OTHER pillar; Saehrimnir the ever-resurrecting boar of Valhalla), other Sindri/Brokkr treasures (Mjolnir, Draupnir -- adjacent-real, own ladders). Wrong owners: not Odin (whose ring is Draupnir), not Thor (whose weapon is Mjolnir).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Yule boar-sacrifice customs in Scandinavia; theology owns why they were dedicated to Freyr.

name: Freyja: cats, falcon-cloak, and the Brisingamen necklace
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The Vanir goddess of love, war, and the pick of the slain. T1: FREYJA is the Vanir goddess of LOVE, BEAUTY, GOLD, SEIDR-MAGIC, and DEATH-IN-BATTLE; she is Freyr's twin sister and daughter of Njord, brought to Asgard with her father and brother as a hostage after the Aesir-Vanir war. Her hall is called FOLKVANGR ('People-Field'); her chariot is drawn by TWO GREAT CATS. Where the cats came from is not told, but Snorri gives them as her team plainly (Gylfaginning 24). T2: her most famous single possession is the necklace BRISINGAMEN, made by FOUR DWARVES named ALFRIGG, DVALIN, BERLING, and GRERR. Freyja saw them making it, wanted it desperately, and paid the price they asked -- she spent one night with each of the four dwarves in return for the necklace (Sorla thattr, in the Flateyjarbok, c. 14th c.; alluded to in Lokasenna 32). It is the single most brilliant piece of jewellery in the Nine Worlds. T3: she also owns a FALCON-CLOAK (valshamr) which any wearer can put on and fly. Loki BORROWS it from her repeatedly -- to fly out and rescue Idunn from the giant Thjazi, and to fly out and find the stolen hammer Mjolnir in Thrym's hall (Skaldskaparmal 3, Thrymskvida 3-5). Freyja lends it (grudgingly, in Thrymskvida). T4: Freyja WEEPS TEARS OF RED GOLD for her wandering husband ODR, who has gone away and left her (Snorri, Gylfaginning 35). She goes searching for him under many names -- MARDOLL, HORN, GEFN, SYR -- across strange peoples. The tears roll down her cheeks and become gold; the poets' kenning for gold is often 'Freyja's tears' (Skaldskaparmal 37). T5: Freyja gets FIRST PICK OF THE SLAIN on any battlefield. Half of the warriors killed in battle go to her hall Folkvangr; the OTHER HALF go to Odin at Valhalla (Grimnismal 14). This is the only case in Norse myth where a warrior might go home to a woman instead of to the All-Father, and the sharing is stated as fact in the Poetic Edda. Freyja gets HER pick FIRST. Further rungs: Loki insults Freyja in Lokasenna by calling her a lover of every god and elf (Lokasenna 30-32) and she is defended by her father; the Sorla thattr version of the Brisingamen story ends with Loki stealing the necklace from her sleeping bedroom in bird-form, and Heimdall recovering it in a seal-fight; her Sunday is FRIDAY (Old English 'Frigedaeg' -- named for her Germanic counterpart Frigg / Freyja).
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 24 (Freyja as Vanir hostage, hall Folkvangr, chariot pulled by cats), Gylfaginning 35 (Freyja weeps gold tears for Odr, searches under many names), Skaldskaparmal 37 (gold kennings from her tears), Skaldskaparmal 3 (Loki borrows her falcon-cloak to rescue Idunn); Poetic Edda, Grimnismal 14 (half the slain go to Freyja, half to Odin), Thrymskvida 3-5 (Loki borrows falcon-cloak), Lokasenna 30-32 (Loki insults Freyja). Sorla thattr (Flateyjarbok, c. 14th c.) for the Brisingamen four-dwarves story. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the number of nights / dwarves for Brisingamen (Sorla thattr says four).

Dinner-test payoff: T5 (Freyja gets FIRST pick of the war-dead, HALF of them, and only THEN does Odin get his half) and T4 (she weeps TEARS OF PURE GOLD for a wandering husband). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Aphrodite's girdle or Isis searching for Osiris -- love-goddess artifacts and love-goddess grief are universal myth patterns. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Norse goddesses (Frigg -- Odin's wife, easily confused with Freyja; SIF -- Thor's wife of the golden hair; SKADI -- ski-goddess and Njord's briefly-wife; IDUNN -- apple-keeper), other named necklaces / cloaks (Loki's falcon-cloak borrowed FROM Freyja), other split-of-the-slain claims (Valkyries choose FOR Odin -- not the same as Freyja's independent claim). name: Tyr: the hand in Fenrir's mouth
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The one-handed god and the wolf he had to lie to, told in Gylfaginning. T1: TYR (Old Norse Tyr; Old English Tiw -- source of TUESDAY) is the Aesir god of WAR and, more importantly, of OATH-KEEPING and law. He is the god warriors call on before battle. He is missing his RIGHT HAND. T2: FENRIR is a monstrous WOLF, child of Loki (with Jormungandr and Hel), raised in Asgard by the gods themselves; he grew SO FAST and SO LARGE that only Tyr was brave enough to walk over each day to feed him (Snorri, Gylfaginning 34). The gods realised Fenrir was going to be too dangerous to leave loose and decided he had to be BOUND. T3: the gods brought Fenrir two great chains -- LAEDING and DROMI -- and told him to try his strength against them; both times he flexed and burst them (Gylfaginning 34). For a THIRD binding they sent Skirnir down to the dark-elves of SVARTALFHEIM, who forged a fetter called GLEIPNIR ('open one'). Gleipnir was made of SIX IMPOSSIBLE THINGS: the FOOTFALL OF A CAT, the BEARD OF A WOMAN, the ROOTS OF A MOUNTAIN, the SINEWS OF A BEAR, the BREATH OF A FISH, and the SPITTLE OF A BIRD (Gylfaginning 34). It came back looking as smooth and soft as a silken ribbon. T4: Fenrir looked at Gleipnir and refused. So light a thing, no glory in bursting it -- and he suspected a trap. He would try it ONLY if one of the gods would put a HAND IN HIS MOUTH as a pledge, to be bitten off if the ribbon turned out to be a fetter. All the gods refused. Only TYR walked forward and put HIS RIGHT HAND between the wolf's jaws (Gylfaginning 34). T5: they bound Fenrir with Gleipnir. He flexed -- and the more he flexed, the TIGHTER Gleipnir became. He could not burst it. In fury he BIT DOWN and took Tyr's right hand off at the wrist. The gods anchored the fetter to a great rock in the deep earth, drove a sword between Fenrir's jaws to keep his mouth open, and left him there to howl at the roots of the world until Ragnarok -- when Gleipnir will finally break and Fenrir will swallow Odin whole (Voluspa 53, Gylfaginning 51). Tyr is one-handed forever after; his hand is the price of the world's binding of the wolf. Further rungs: TUESDAY is named after Tyr's Germanic form Tiw (Old English Tiwesdaeg); the six impossible ingredients of Gleipnir are the Norse explanation for why cats have soundless feet, women have no beards, mountains have no roots, bears no visible sinews, fish no visible breath, birds no visible spittle (Gylfaginning 34 -- the ingredients WERE USED UP making the ribbon); at Ragnarok Tyr will fight the hound GARM before Helheim, and each will kill the other.
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 34 (Fenrir raised in Asgard, only Tyr feeds him, three chains Laeding/Dromi/Gleipnir, six impossible ingredients, Tyr's right hand as pledge, hand bitten off); Gylfaginning 25 (Tyr as god of war, missing hand); Gylfaginning 51 (Ragnarok -- Tyr against Garm, Fenrir against Odin); Poetic Edda, Voluspa 53 (Fenrir devours Odin). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the six ingredients exactly in order (Snorri's list: fjallsins raetr, konu skegg, bjarnar sinar, fisks andi, fugls hraki, kattar dynr).

Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Gleipnir was made of a CAT'S FOOTFALL, a WOMAN'S BEARD, the ROOTS OF A MOUNTAIN, a BEAR'S SINEWS, a FISH'S BREATH, a BIRD'S SPITTLE) and T4 (Tyr put his OWN RIGHT HAND in the wolf's mouth so the wolf would let itself be bound). Use the six ingredients as their OWN rung -- it's a memorable named list. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Prometheus chained by Zeus or of the demon Asmodeus bound by Solomon -- binding-a-monster is a universal myth pattern. Tyr's sacrifice is the Norse cousin of Odin's eye -- god pays with body-part for the world's safety. Wrong day: not Wednesday (Odin/Woden) not Thursday (Thor).

name: The death of Baldr: mistletoe and the blind brother
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The killing that starts the countdown to Ragnarok, told most fully in Snorri's Gylfaginning 49. T1: BALDR is the FAIREST of the gods, son of Odin and Frigg, so bright and good that no one in Asgard can speak against him; he lives in the hall BREIDABLIK ('Broad-Shining') where nothing unclean is allowed (Gylfaginning 22, 49). He begins to have BAD DREAMS -- dreams of his own death. T2: his mother FRIGG, terrified, goes out across the nine worlds and makes EVERY THING SWEAR AN OATH not to harm Baldr -- fire, water, iron, stone, sicknesses, poisons, snakes, birds, beasts, trees. Everything swears (Gylfaginning 49). To celebrate, the gods invent a game: they set Baldr in the middle of the ring and take turns throwing weapons at him -- swords, spears, arrows, stones -- and everything MISSES OR BOUNCES OFF, because everything has sworn. It becomes the entertainment of Asgard. T3: LOKI is envious. He goes to Frigg in disguise as an old woman and asks conversationally whether truly EVERY THING has sworn. Frigg answers freely -- yes, everything, only she did NOT bother a little plant called MISTLETOE, growing on an oak west of Valhalla, because it seemed too young to demand oaths from (Gylfaginning 49). T4: Loki goes to the oak, plucks the mistletoe, and takes it back to the ring where the game is being played. Baldr's BLIND brother HODR is standing off to one side, unable to join in because he cannot see to throw. Loki puts the mistletoe SHAFT in Hodr's hand and offers to guide his aim. Hodr throws. The dart of mistletoe pierces Baldr straight through, and Baldr falls dead (Gylfaginning 49). It is the greatest disaster the gods have ever known -- and they cannot even TAKE VENGEANCE, because Asgard is a sanctuary and no blood may be shed there. T5: Odin sends his other son HERMODR down to HEL on Sleipnir, riding NINE NIGHTS through valleys 'deep and dark' until he leaps the fence into the death-realm. Hel agrees to release Baldr if -- and only if -- 'EVERY THING IN THE WORLD BOTH LIVING AND DEAD WILL WEEP FOR HIM' (Gylfaginning 49). Messengers go out. All things weep -- gods, giants, men, animals, stones, trees, metals (Snorri says this is why the metals still weep when brought out of the cold into the warmth -- condensation). But in a cave sits one giantess, THOKK ('Thanks'), and when the messengers ask her to weep for Baldr she answers with the mocking little verse: 'Thokk will weep dry tears at Baldr's bale-fire; not in life, not in death, did the churl's son give me joy; let Hel keep what she has' (Gylfaginning 49). Because ONE creature will not weep, Baldr stays with Hel until the end of the world. And Snorri adds: 'people say that Thokk was Loki.' Further rungs: Baldr's funeral is on the great ship RINGHORNI, which is so heavy the giantess Hyrrokkin has to shove it out (Thor almost kills her); Baldr's wife NANNA dies of grief on the pyre and is burned with him; his horse is led to the pyre too, harness and all; the RING DRAUPNIR (Odin's arm-ring that drops eight copies of itself every ninth night) is laid on Baldr's chest and goes to Hel with him.
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 49 (the entire death-of-Baldr sequence -- dreams, Frigg's oaths from everything, the mistletoe missed, Loki as the old woman, Hodr guided to throw, Baldr dies, Hermodr rides Sleipnir to Hel, all things weep except the giantess Thokk = Loki, Baldr stays); Poetic Edda, Voluspa 31-35 (the mistletoe, Hodr, the avenger Vali) and Baldrs Draumar (whole poem -- Odin's descent to a dead volva to learn Baldr's fate). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Baldr' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Baldr', 'Hodr', 'Hermodr', 'Baldrs draumar' -- fair Aesir, bad dreams, Frigg's oaths, mistletoe overlooked, Loki as old woman asking Frigg, Hodr the blind brother, Hermodr's ride to Hel, Hel's condition of universal weeping, Thokk refuses = Loki. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: Snorri's exact wording of Thokk's verse.

Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Loki dressed as an OLD WOMAN and asked Frigg if literally everything had sworn -- and she named MISTLETOE) and T5 (all things wept for Baldr except ONE giantess in a cave who said 'let Hel keep what she has' -- and the giantess was LOKI). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'killed by mistletoe' AND ask what killed Baldr; describe the SCENE (a shining god at the centre of a ring, weapons bouncing off him harmlessly, a blind brother off to the side, a dart guided into his hand) and let the recall be MISTLETOE, HODR, the OLD WOMAN'S TRUE IDENTITY, or the giantess who would not weep. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the Passion of Christ or the death of Achilles -- a dying-god story is the emotional peak of every myth-cycle. The Christian-parallel-hunt should be RESISTED; this is Norse. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Norse deaths (Baldr's mother Nanna dies on the pyre, Odin himself will die at Ragnarok, Thor of Jormungandr's poison), other Loki disguises (mare, salmon, falcon-cloak, fly, old woman -- rich list), other plants (Balder-flower / mayweed is 'Baldr's brow' in the sagas, not the killer). Wrong killer of Baldr: not Hodr willingly -- he was BLIND and GUIDED.
history_overlap: No place overlap (Breidablik / Hel are mythic). ANIMAL bank might own mistletoe as a plant; theology owns why it killed a god.

name: Heimdallr: Gjallarhorn and grass growing
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The god of the rainbow-bridge and how he stays awake. T1: HEIMDALLR (also spelled Heimdall) is the WATCHMAN of the gods, the god who stands guard at the rainbow-bridge BIFROST, which connects Asgard to Midgard. He is the son of Odin -- and, mysteriously, of NINE MOTHERS (Voluspa hin skamma, quoted in Gylfaginning 27; also the poem Heimdalargaldr, now lost, quoted by Snorri as saying he was born of nine sisters). T2: he needs LESS SLEEP than a bird. He can SEE for a hundred leagues by day or night. He can HEAR THE GRASS GROWING in the fields, and the WOOL GROWING on the backs of sheep (Snorri, Gylfaginning 27). No one gets past him. T3: his weapon and instrument is a great horn called GJALLARHORN ('Yelling Horn'), whose blast can be heard through ALL NINE WORLDS. The horn is kept under the roots of Yggdrasil beside Mimir's well until the moment it is needed (Voluspa 27, 46; Gylfaginning 15). T4: Heimdallr will blow Gjallarhorn ONCE -- at the very start of RAGNAROK, when the giants at last cross Bifrost coming for the gods. That single blast is the signal for the end of the world -- every Aesir hears it, every giant hears it, every dead man in Valhalla hears it and takes up his weapon (Voluspa 46; Gylfaginning 51). T5: at Ragnarok itself Heimdallr and LOKI meet on the field and KILL EACH OTHER -- these two are lifelong enemies (in one older story Heimdallr in seal-form wrestles Loki in seal-form off a rock to recover Freyja's stolen necklace Brisingamen; see the Freyja ladder), and the ending of that hostility is that both fall together (Gylfaginning 51). Heimdallr's home is called HIMINBJORG ('Sky-Cliff') at the top of Bifrost; his sacred horse is GULLTOPPR ('Golden-Top'); he is one of the very few Norse gods with a mostly WHITE colour association ('the white god'). Further rungs: Heimdallr is also called RIGR in the poem Rigsthula, in which he walks the earth in disguise, sleeps three nights with three different couples, and fathers the three CLASSES of humankind (thralls, farmers, and jarls); the horn's blast is the Norse equivalent of the last trumpet.

name: Idunn and the golden apples: kidnapped by Thjazi
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: How the gods almost lost their youth, told in Snorri's Skaldskaparmal 2. T1: IDUNN is the Aesir goddess who keeps a wooden ASH-BOX of GOLDEN APPLES; the gods eat one apple each and stay YOUNG. Without her apples the Aesir would grow old and die. Her husband is the poet-god BRAGI. T2: one day Odin, Loki, and Hoenir are travelling in Jotunheim and try to roast an ox they've killed. The fire won't cook it. A great EAGLE lands in the tree above them and admits it is stopping the meat from cooking -- and will let it roast only if they share the meal. When the eagle takes the largest cuts, Loki grabs a staff to beat him off; the staff STICKS to the eagle and Loki's hands STICK to the staff, and Loki is dragged up into the air over the rocks. The eagle is really the giant THJAZI in disguise (Skaldskaparmal 2). T3: To be set down, Loki must swear an oath to bring IDUNN AND HER APPLES out of Asgard for Thjazi. Loki agrees. Back in Asgard he coaxes Idunn into a wood outside the walls, promising to show her apples that grow there just like her own -- and Thjazi swoops in as an eagle again and CARRIES HER OFF to his home in Jotunheim, apples and all (Skaldskaparmal 2). T4: without Idunn's apples the gods begin to GROW OLD -- silver hair, stiff joints, blurred eyes. They call council; they realise Loki was the last one seen with Idunn. They give Loki a choice: bring her back or die. Loki borrows FREYJA'S FALCON-CLOAK, flies to Thjazi's hall, and while Thjazi is out fishing turns Idunn into a NUT and carries her back in his talons (Skaldskaparmal 2). T5: Thjazi returns, sees Idunn gone, takes eagle-form and CHASES Loki back to Asgard. The gods see them coming; they pile SHAVINGS at the wall, wait until Loki with his nut is over the wall, and set the shavings ALIGHT. Thjazi's wings catch fire; he falls inside the walls and the Aesir kill him (Skaldskaparmal 2). Idunn is restored, and the apples come back. Thjazi's daughter SKADI comes to Asgard to demand blood-money -- she gets to pick a husband from among the gods by looking at their FEET only, and mistakenly chooses NJORD (Freyr's father, thinking he was Baldr because his feet were so clean); Odin flings Thjazi's EYES into the sky, where they become TWO STARS. Further rungs: this is Loki's first big betrayal of the Aesir (he sets it up AND resolves it -- classic Loki); Skadi is bad at marriage (Njord loves the sea, she loves the mountains, they separate); the two eye-stars are unspecified in Snorri but modern commentators guess the Gemini.
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Skaldskaparmal 2 (whole story -- ox will not cook, Thjazi as eagle, Loki's staff stuck, oath to bring Idunn out, Loki coaxes Idunn into the wood, Thjazi carries her off, gods grow old, Loki borrows Freyja's falcon-cloak, Idunn as a nut, Thjazi in pursuit, wing-shavings burnt at the wall, Skadi's compensation, husband-by-feet, Thjazi's eyes as stars); Poetic Edda, Haustlong (skaldic poem by Thjodolf of Hvin describing this same story in kennings). DISTRACTOR MINE: other 'apples of youth / immortality' (Hesperides -- Greek pillar; the golden apple of discord -- also Greek), other Loki shape-shifts (mare, salmon, fly, old woman -- adjacent, own ladders), other kidnapped goddesses (Persephone -- other pillar; Freyja demanded as ransom -- SEE Thrymskvida ladder). Wrong bird-form: not raven (Odin's), not swan.

name: The Norns at the well of Urd
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The three fate-women who set the lives of gods and men, told in Voluspa and Gylfaginning. T1: beneath the second root of YGGDRASIL lies a well called URDARBRUNNR, 'the well of URD'. Beside the well live THREE maidens who set the fates of every child born into the world -- gods, giants, elves, humans, dwarves alike. They are the NORNS (Voluspa 20; Gylfaginning 15). T2: their names are URD, VERDANDI, and SKULD -- literally 'WAS', 'BEING', and 'SHALL-BE' (Old Norse Urdr = past, Verdandi = becoming, Skuld = will-be). Together they are what has happened, what is happening, and what is yet to happen (Voluspa 20). T3: they carve laws onto WOODEN TABLETS and set the lives of every child; whatever they carve stands, and no god can undo it (Voluspa 20). Some later poets add that they WEAVE the threads of fate on great looms and CUT them at death; the older Voluspa image is carving on wood rather than weaving. T4: every day the three Norns take WHITE CLAY from the well of Urd and CARRY WATER UP from the well to POUR OVER THE ROOTS of the world-tree Yggdrasil, so that the tree stays alive and does not wither (Gylfaginning 16). The white slurry stains everything it touches -- and Snorri says that is why the surface of eggshells, and the film on a fresh apple, are that milky-pale colour: it is Urd's water. T5: the Norns are OLDER THAN THE GODS. The Voluspa says that the ORLOG -- the primary Norse word for FATE, meaning literally 'ancient-law' -- was laid down BY THE NORNS before the gods came into their power (Voluspa 20). The Aesir act inside a story the Norns have already written. Even Odin cannot untie a Norn's carving; even Thor's hammer will not shatter one. There are also LESSER norns beside the three great ones, some good and some ill, who visit new-born children as attendants; a poor man's ill-luck is his lesser-norns' work (Gylfaginning 15). Further rungs: the three Greek Moirai (Clotho, Lachesis, Atropos) and the three Anglo-Saxon Wyrd sisters are the same fate-triad idea; the Voluspa is spoken by a VOLVA (a seeress) who has personally seen the Norns at the well; Skuld the youngest Norn is sometimes said also to lead the Valkyries into battle.
source: PRIMARY: Poetic Edda, Voluspa 19-20 (Yggdrasil, the well of Urd, the three maidens who set the laws for all the ages of men); Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 15-16 (three Norns at the well, the naming Urd/Verdandi/Skuld, the water carried up to preserve Yggdrasil, the white clay that makes eggshells and fresh-apple film pale, lesser norns visiting babies). No 'primitive'. name: Yggdrasil: the world-tree and its residents
strand: Norse: Aesir gods and their world
scope: The single most important image in Norse cosmology, told across Voluspa, Grimnismal, and Gylfaginning. T1: YGGDRASIL is a giant ASH TREE at the centre of the Norse cosmos. Its branches spread over all the worlds; its three ROOTS drink from three different wells; on it hangs everything that is (Gylfaginning 15-16; Grimnismal 29-35; Voluspa 19). The name means 'YGG'S HORSE' -- Ygg 'the Terrible' is Odin, and the tree became his gallows on the night he hanged himself for the runes (see that ladder). T2: the tree has THREE GREAT ROOTS. One reaches down to the well of URD, where the Norns sit (see the Norns ladder). One reaches to MIMIR'S WELL, where Odin traded his eye (see that ladder). The third reaches down into NIFLHEIM, the cold mist-world at the northern end, where the well HVERGELMIR bubbles and the eleven ice-rivers ELIVAGAR flow (Grimnismal 26-27, Gylfaginning 15). T3: many creatures live in the tree. At the TOP sits an unnamed EAGLE, wise and huge, with a HAWK called VEDRFOLNIR perched between its eyes. Four HARTS (stags) named DAINN, DVALINN, DUNEYRR, and DURATHROR pace around the branches nibbling the leaves. A GOAT named HEIDRUN stands on the roof of Valhalla eating leaves off Yggdrasil, and her milk becomes MEAD that the Einherjar in Valhalla drink from her udder forever (Grimnismal 25, 33; Gylfaginning 39-40). T4: at the BOTTOM of the third root, gnawing at it, lies the DRAGON NIDHOGG, 'Malice-Striker', who chews at the root day and night trying to bring the whole tree down. Between the dragon at the bottom and the eagle at the top runs an ETERNAL BEEF between them, and the messenger between them is a SQUIRREL called RATATOSK ('Drill-Tooth') who runs up and down the trunk carrying INSULTS from one to the other, keeping the quarrel going (Grimnismal 32; Gylfaginning 16). T5: the three roots feed the tree because the Norns pour water on them, but the tree is still ALWAYS DYING -- 'more troubles than men know afflict Yggdrasil' (Grimnismal 35): the hart gnaws its leaves, the dragon gnaws its root, the sides rot. Yet it stands -- and it will STILL STAND after Ragnarok. When the fire of Surt sweeps the world and burns everything else, one man and one woman named LIF and LIFTHRASIR will HIDE INSIDE YGGDRASIL and survive the ending, then step out to repopulate the reborn world (Vafthrudnismal 45). Yggdrasil is the ONE thing that outlasts the end. Further rungs: the tree connects the NINE WORLDS (Asgard, Vanaheim, Alfheim, Midgard, Jotunheim, Nidavellir, Svartalfheim, Muspelheim, Niflheim / Helheim -- there is scholarly overlap on whether it is nine or the count starts elsewhere); the goat Heidrun's endless mead-udder is the source of Valhalla's supply; Ratatosk the squirrel is beloved of children everywhere and is one of the most cited details in modern retellings.
source: PRIMARY: Poetic Edda, Voluspa 19 (the world-ash Yggdrasil), Grimnismal 25-35 (the tree's residents -- Heidrun the goat, the four harts, Nidhogg the dragon at the root, the unnamed eagle with Vedrfolnir the hawk between his eyes, Ratatosk carrying insults up and down), Vafthrudnismal 45 (Lif and Lifthrasir surviving in the tree at Ragnarok); Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 15-16 (three roots to Urd, Mimir, Niflheim; residents; the tree always suffering), Gylfaginning 39-40 (Heidrun and Eikthyrnir the stag). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (a DRAGON at the root, an EAGLE at the top, and a SQUIRREL running INSULTS between them all day) and T5 (when the world ENDS, one MAN and one WOMAN hide INSIDE the tree and survive to repopulate it). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the world-tree Yggdrasil' AND ask what tree; describe the SCENE (three deep roots at three separate wells, a squirrel running the trunk, four stags nibbling the branches) and let the recall be YGGDRASIL, the squirrel's NAME, or the two humans who survive inside it. Use the residents as MANY separate rungs (eagle, dragon, harts, Heidrun, Ratatosk, Lif and Lifthrasir). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the Tree of Life in Genesis or the tree in Buddhist cosmology -- world-tree is a universal myth pattern; the Norse version has the RICHEST cast of residents. DISTRACTOR MINE: other named tree-things (the oak at Dodona for Zeus's oracle -- Greek; the Tree of Knowledge in Eden -- Christian), other named squirrels (the ONLY named squirrel in Norse myth is Ratatosk -- easy false-choice space), other dragons (Fafnir the Volsung's-gold dragon -- Norse but different; Jormungandr the Midgard Serpent is a serpent not a dragon), other apocalypse-survivors (Deucalion and Pyrrha -- Greek; Noah -- Christian). Wrong tree-kind: Yggdrasil is an ASH specifically, not an oak or a yew.
